transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Yeah, hi. Um… I guess what brought me in is that people keep telling me I’m not listening. Like my supervisor will be talking right to me, or my wife will be telling me something, and then a minute later I realize I only got maybe half of what they said. Then I’m asking them to repeat it, and they get frustrated.

It’s not like I’m trying to ignore them, you know? I’ll be looking at them, even, and then somehow I miss parts of it. It’s been causing problems.
Do you think you're having trouble hearing what people say?

I don’t know if it’s my hearing exactly. I mean, I can hear sounds fine, I think—like at work I hear the machines, and at home I hear the TV when it’s on in the other room, which actually drives my wife crazy because I’ll notice that but then miss what she said right to me.

So… maybe not hearing like my ears, but I’m not totally sure. It feels more like I catch some words and then my mind is somewhere else, but I don’t know how to explain it.
Is it harder for you to understand what people are saying when there’s background noise?

Maybe, but honestly the bigger thing is… even when it’s quiet, like my wife can be right in front of me talking, or my supervisor at work is looking straight at me, and then a minute later I realize I only got like half of it. Then I’m asking them to repeat themselves, and they get annoyed.

I mean, noise probably doesn’t help, especially at work, but it’s not just that. It’s like I’m there, but I miss chunks of what they said.
Have you had this kind of trouble paying attention when people talk to you since you were a child?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, back in school it was kind of a thing. Teachers were always moving my seat around, like putting me up front or away from certain kids, because I couldn’t really stay put and I’d be messing with stuff or jumping in.

I remember calling out answers before I was supposed to, too. And before middle school, I’d get in trouble for butting into other kids’ work, like if they were doing something wrong I’d just lean over and start telling them, or sometimes take over. Not because I was trying to be a jerk, I just… I don’t know, I’d jump in before thinking. So yeah, it goes way back.
Do you have the same trouble staying focused in situations other than conversations, like when reading, doing paperwork, or following through on tasks?

I’m not sure. I mean, reading… I don’t read a lot, honestly. Paperwork at work, there’s some stuff, but usually I just kind of get through what I have to get through.

Tasks, I don’t know—depends what kind of task you mean. Like at home, I’ll start doing something and then my wife will ask me to do something else, or the dog needs to go out, and then suddenly I’m fixing a drawer or looking for a tool I swear I just had. But I don’t know if that’s “focus” exactly or just normal life getting in the way.

Sorry, what was the main part you were asking—reading and paperwork?
Do you often start a task and then get pulled off it before you finish?

I mean… I guess sometimes? It depends what you count as “pulled off.” Like if I’m doing something and someone asks me something, yeah, I’ll stop, but then sometimes I go back to it.

At work it’s different because the line kind of tells you what’s next, you know? You can’t just wander off too much or somebody’s yelling. At home, though, it’s more like… I’ll be doing one thing and then notice something else, but I don’t know if that’s what you mean.

Like yesterday I went to grab something from the garage and then I was looking at this box of old cords because I thought one of them might fit the radio in my truck—sorry, that’s probably not what you’re asking. So… yeah, maybe, but I’m not sure how often.
When someone is talking to you, is it easier to understand them if you can see their face?

Uh… I don’t know if I’ve really paid attention to that. Maybe? Like if I can see somebody, I guess it helps just because I know they’re talking to me, but I don’t think I’m, like, reading lips or anything.

Sometimes if someone’s talking from another room I miss stuff, but then again my wife talks to me from the kitchen while I’m in the garage and there’s the washer going, or the dog’s barking, and I’m trying to find—sorry. Yeah, I’m not sure. I haven’t really noticed whether seeing their face makes a big difference.
Do you often forget everyday things, like appointments, errands, or where you put your keys or phone?

I mean… I’m not sure how to answer that. I do misplace stuff sometimes, like everybody does, but I don’t know if it’s “often.” My wife would probably have a better answer, honestly.

Appointments, I usually try to put them in my phone, but then if I don’t put it in right away… anyway, errands depend. Like if I’m going to the store, I’ll remember three things and then get home and realize I didn’t get the one thing I actually went for—but then sometimes the store moves everything around and I get annoyed and just grab whatever. 

Keys and phone, yeah, I look for them, but I don’t know if it’s more than normal. What were the examples again—appointments and keys?
How often do you lose things you need, like your keys, phone, wallet, or tools?

Yeah, I mean… I do lose track of stuff, but I don’t know how often is “often.” My phone, I’ll set it down somewhere dumb, like on top of the dryer or in the truck, and then I’m walking around patting my pockets like an idiot.

Tools are harder because at work they’ve got places they’re supposed to go, and if someone else grabs something then I’m looking for it and getting mad, but it’s not always me, you know? At home I’ll be in the middle of fixing something and put the screwdriver down, then I’m opening drawers, checking the garage, and then I find it right where I was standing. But I don’t know if that counts as losing it or just being busy.
When people talk to you, do the words sound muffled or unclear?

Um… muffled? I don’t think so. Not usually. I mean, if there’s a bunch of noise going on, then yeah, anybody sounds kind of garbled, right? Like at work if the machines are running and someone’s trying to tell me something from across the line, I’m like, “What?” But I don’t know if that’s the words being unclear or just… there’s a forklift backing up and someone dropped a pallet and everybody’s talking at once.

If we’re just sitting here talking, I don’t notice the words sounding muffled. I might miss something if I’m not—if there’s too much going on, but the words themselves don’t sound weird to me.
Do you often leave tasks unfinished, even after you’ve started them?

Uh… unfinished? I’m not sure. I mean, I’ll start something and then if something else comes up, I might step away from it, but I don’t know if I’d say I “often” leave it unfinished.

Like at home, I’ll be doing something and then my wife asks me about the trash or the dog’s water bowl or whatever, and then I’m in the garage looking for something else, and next thing I know I’m dealing with a completely different thing. But sometimes I do go back and finish the first thing. Sometimes.

At work it’s different because stuff has to get done, you know? The line doesn’t really care if you feel like finishing or not. So… I guess it depends what you mean by unfinished. Like unfinished for the day, or just I got pulled off it?
Do you often have trouble following through on instructions?

Following through on instructions… I don’t know. I mean, if somebody gives me like one thing, sure, I can do that. But if it’s a whole list, sometimes I’ll do the first part and then I’m thinking about the second part, and then someone else comes over asking about something, and now I’m on that.

But I don’t know if that’s me not following through or just the way things go. Like at work, people act like they told you something clear, but they’ll say it while walking away, or there’s noise, or they change it five minutes later. Then later it’s like, “Why didn’t you do that?” and I’m thinking, well, you didn’t exactly lay it out like a recipe.

At home too, my wife will tell me something, and I’ll be like, “Yeah, yeah,” but then I’m doing another thing already. So… maybe? I guess I’d say it happens, but I’m not really sure how often you mean.
When someone is talking to you and you miss part of it, do you usually realize your mind had drifted away?

Yeah… sometimes I do realize it after the fact. Like someone will be talking right to me—my supervisor, or my wife—and I’m looking at them and everything, but then a minute later I’m like, wait, I only caught half of that.

And then I have to ask them to repeat it, which gets old fast. My wife especially gets irritated, like, “Were you even listening?” And I was, sort of… or I thought I was. But then my head’s on some other thing, or I’m watching what’s going on behind them, and suddenly I missed the middle part.

That’s kind of why I came in, honestly. People keep saying I’m not listening, and I don’t always know it until I realize I can’t answer what they just said.
Do you ever fail to notice everyday sounds, like the doorbell, your phone ringing, or someone calling your name?

I don’t know about the doorbell or phone so much… I mean, maybe, but what I notice more is people talking right to me and then I miss it.

Like my wife or my supervisor will be saying something straight to my face, and I’m looking at them, but then a minute later I realize I only caught half of what they said. Then I’m asking, “Wait, what was that again?” and people get annoyed. That’s kind of what brought me in, honestly—everybody keeps saying I’m not listening.
Do you often feel restless, like you have a hard time sitting still?

Yeah. I mean… sitting still is hard. It’s not just boredom, it’s like this pressure starts building up in me, like in my chest and my legs, and I feel like I have to move or do something right then.

Like if I’m stuck sitting there too long, I start feeling like I’m gonna crawl out of my skin. And then I’m thinking about getting up, shifting around, anything. It’s funny, because some people can just sit through stuff like it’s nothing, but for me it feels like my body is arguing with the chair.
Do you often feel driven to keep moving, like you can’t stay seated when you’re expected to?

Yeah, pretty much all the time. From when I clock in at work, it’s like I’m already going from one thing to the next—work orders, then thinking about pickup, then dinner, laundry, whatever else needs doing.

And even if there’s, like, a quiet minute where technically I could sit down, I don’t really do that. I’ll get up and check something, move stuff around, start another task. My wife will be like, “Just sit for a second,” and I’m thinking, yeah, I should, but I can’t seem to actually rest. It feels like I’m always supposed to be moving to the next thing.
Do you often not notice sounds like your phone ringing or the doorbell, even when it’s otherwise quiet?

I’m not really sure on that one. Like, I don’t think I’m sitting in a quiet room and just totally missing the doorbell or my phone ringing… at least not that I’ve noticed.

The phone thing is tricky though, because half the time it’s on vibrate or it’s buried under stuff, and then I’ll find it later and there’s missed calls, but that’s not really the same, right? And the doorbell—I mean, we don’t get that many people coming by anyway. Mostly packages, and those guys barely ring it, they just drop it and disappear.

So… I guess I can’t really say that happens a lot. I don’t have a clear example of it.
Is it hard for you to hear what people are saying in a group conversation?

Yeah… in groups, sometimes, but honestly it’s even when it’s just one person talking right at me. That’s kind of what made me come in, because people keep saying I’m not listening.

Like my supervisor will be giving me something I need to do, or my wife will be telling me something, and I’m standing there looking at them, I’m not trying to ignore them, but then a minute later I realize I only caught half of what they said. Then I’m asking, “Wait, what was that again?” and they get irritated because from their side it looks like I just didn’t care enough to listen.

In a group it’s probably worse, because there’s more talking going on and I kind of lose the thread, but yeah… the main thing is I’ll think I’m listening and then realize I missed chunks of it.

Yeah… sometimes I do realize it after the fact. Like someone will be talking right to me—my supervisor, or my wife—and I’m looking at them and everything, but then a minute later I’m like, wait, I only caught half of that.

And then I have to ask them to repeat it, which gets old fast. My wife especially gets irritated, like, “Were you even listening?” And I was, sort of… or I thought I was. But then my head’s on some other thing, or I’m watching what’s going on behind them, and suddenly I missed the middle part.

That’s kind of why I came in, honestly. People keep saying I’m not listening, and I don’t always know it until I realize I can’t answer what they just said.

doctor.intent: Differentiate attentional lapses from hearing loss by asking whether the patient also misses nonverbal sounds in daily life.
doctor.question: Do you ever fail to notice everyday sounds, like the doorbell, your phone ringing, or someone calling your name?

target_item.name: Listening_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: What brought me in is people keep saying I’m not listening—my supervisor or my wife will be talking straight to me, and a minute later I realize I only caught half of it and I’m asking them to say it again.
target_item.reason: The question is about not noticing someone calling your name or missing auditory cues, which most directly matches difficulty seeming to listen when spoken to directly.

patient.answer:
I don’t know about the doorbell or phone so much… I mean, maybe, but what I notice more is people talking right to me and then I miss it.

Like my wife or my supervisor will be saying something straight to my face, and I’m looking at them, but then a minute later I realize I only caught half of what they said. Then I’m asking, “Wait, what was that again?” and people get annoyed. That’s kind of what brought me in, honestly—everybody keeps saying I’m not listening.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is clinically significant hyperactivity/restlessness in adulthood to distinguish ADHD from a nonspecific attention complaint or hearing problem.
doctor.question: Do you often feel restless, like you have a hard time sitting still?

target_item.name: Feeling_Restless
target_item.manifestation: When I have to sit still, it feels like pressure building up inside my chest and legs, like I’ve got to move or do something right now or I’ll crawl out of my skin.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about feeling restless and having a hard time sitting still.

patient.answer:
Yeah. I mean… sitting still is hard. It’s not just boredom, it’s like this pressure starts building up in me, like in my chest and my legs, and I feel like I have to move or do something right then.

Like if I’m stuck sitting there too long, I start feeling like I’m gonna crawl out of my skin. And then I’m thinking about getting up, shifting around, anything. It’s funny, because some people can just sit through stuff like it’s nothing, but for me it feels like my body is arguing with the chair.

inference.note: Restlessness/hard time sitting still adds another hyperactivity symptom, increasing support for F90.0. Hearing loss remains less likely given no muffled speech or broad missed environmental sounds, but not fully ruled out yet.

doctor.intent: Determine whether he currently shows another core ADHD hyperactive symptom, which best separates ADHD from isolated inattention or hearing problems.
doctor.question: Do you often feel driven to keep moving, like you can’t stay seated when you’re expected to?

target_item.name: Constant_Activity
target_item.manifestation: From the time I clock in until I get home, I’m always jumping to the next thing—work orders, pickup, dinner, laundry—and even when there’s a quiet minute I can’t just sit down and rest.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feeling driven to keep moving, which directly matches being constantly active or acting as if driven by a motor.

patient.answer:
Yeah, pretty much all the time. From when I clock in at work, it’s like I’m already going from one thing to the next—work orders, then thinking about pickup, then dinner, laundry, whatever else needs doing.

And even if there’s, like, a quiet minute where technically I could sit down, I don’t really do that. I’ll get up and check something, move stuff around, start another task. My wife will be like, “Just sit for a second,” and I’m thinking, yeah, I should, but I can’t seem to actually rest. It feels like I’m always supposed to be moving to the next thing.

inference.note: Restlessness since childhood, difficulty staying seated, impulsivity/calling out, interrupting, distractibility during conversations, losing things, and trouble following multi-step instructions strongly support ADHD combined presentation; R41.840 is subsumed. Hearing loss not fully excluded but is less supported by intact perception of sounds and absence of muffled speech.

doctor.intent: Differentiate inattention from hearing loss by determining whether the patient misses non-speech sounds in everyday life.
doctor.question: Do you often not notice sounds like your phone ringing or the doorbell, even when it’s otherwise quiet?

target_item.reason: The question is specifically about not noticing environmental sounds like a phone ringing or doorbell, which is not covered by the listed symptom profile; S003 is about difficulty listening when spoken to directly.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure on that one. Like, I don’t think I’m sitting in a quiet room and just totally missing the doorbell or my phone ringing… at least not that I’ve noticed.

The phone thing is tricky though, because half the time it’s on vibrate or it’s buried under stuff, and then I’ll find it later and there’s missed calls, but that’s not really the same, right? And the doorbell—I mean, we don’t get that many people coming by anyway. Mostly packages, and those guys barely ring it, they just drop it and disappear.

So… I guess I can’t really say that happens a lot. I don’t have a clear example of it.

doctor.intent: Differentiate inattentive listening from true hearing loss by testing for increased difficulty hearing in groups or noisy environments, which would support hearing impairment more than ADHD.
doctor.question: Is it hard for you to hear what people are saying in a group conversation?

target_item.name: Listening_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: What brought me in is people keep saying I’m not listening—my supervisor or my wife will be talking straight to me, and a minute later I realize I only caught half of it and I’m asking them to say it again.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about difficulty taking in what people are saying during conversation, which most closely matches the listening difficulty symptom.

patient.answer:
Yeah… in groups, sometimes, but honestly it’s even when it’s just one person talking right at me. That’s kind of what made me come in, because people keep saying I’m not listening.

Like my supervisor will be giving me something I need to do, or my wife will be telling me something, and I’m standing there looking at them, I’m not trying to ignore them, but then a minute later I realize I only caught half of what they said. Then I’m asking, “Wait, what was that again?” and they get irritated because from their side it looks like I just didn’t care enough to listen.

In a group it’s probably worse, because there’s more talking going on and I kind of lose the thread, but yeah… the main thing is I’ll think I’m listening and then realize I missed chunks of it.

inference.note: Consistent lifelong inattention plus hyperactivity/restlessness and impulsive childhood behaviors support ADHD combined presentation; repeated denial of muffled/unclear speech, no clear missed everyday sounds in quiet, and primary problem being mind drifting rather than audibility make hearing loss less likely.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main concern in their own words to begin narrowing the diagnosis
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The interview supports ADHD, combined presentation: persistent symptoms since childhood across settings with both inattention (especially not seeming to listen, mind drifting during direct conversation, distractibility, difficulty with multi-step instructions, misplacing items) and hyperactive/impulsive features (restlessness, inability to sit still, feeling driven to keep moving, childhood blurting out and intruding). Hearing/perceptual disorder is less supported because the patient reports words are not muffled and problems occur even in quiet settings due to attention drifting. Symptoms are causing interpersonal and occupational problems.
